newsitem.title: USA: N.Y. Assembly wants to hold health cuts at $96 mln.
newsitem.headline: N.Y. Assembly wants to hold health cuts at $96 mln.

text.p: The New York State Assembly, which last year only accepted about $2 out of every $7 of healthcare cuts proposed by Gov George Pataki, started this year's battle by turning down a slight bigger proportion.

While the Republican governor, after being criticized, added back about $100 million of the $913 million healthcare cuts he initially put forward, he has said that getting a balanced budget hinged on more steep healthcare reductions.

The Democrat-led Assembly, which has projected more than twice the $860 million surplus Pataki sees for fiscal 1998, also wants to end a cost-cutting process that gives healthcare providers inflation adjustments, according to its own version of a budget that it approved last week.

"It restores almost all the Governor's Medicaid cuts and in one respect, even rolls back part of what we did last year," Assemblyman Richard Gottfried, D-Manhattan, who chairs the health committee, said on Friday. "The governor proposed not doing an inflation factor, and we rejected that."
Gov. George Pataki has blasted the Assembly's budget plan for raising spending by about $4.7 billion, and the state for the 13th year in a row missed its April 1 deadline for approving a budget pact.
A spokesman for Pataki was not immediately available to comment.
Even though the Assembly turned down all but about $96 million of Pataki's approximately $820 million of healthcare cuts, its new plan would only add $250 million to next year's budget.

"We have knocked down the governor's estimate of how much the existing program will cost by a couple of hundred million dollars," Gottfried said, explaining that the Assembly's estimates were smaller because it sees less inflation in the healthcare industry.

Also, the Assembly looks for the drop in welfare rolls to cut the number of Medicaid recipients more than Pataki, Gottfried said, explaining that even though people who no longer are collecting welfare still may qualify for Medicaid, they do not always re-apply for the program, as required.
The amount of cuts the Assembly said it was willing to accept for next year was less than half of the approximately $220 million of reductions it agreed to last year.

Gottfried, noting that the size of any cuts made by New York State has to be multiplied about three times to reflect how much federal and local aid also is lost, stressed the importance of protecting the state's healthcare in an increasingly competitive arena.

"Healthcare providers of almost all categories are under increasing financial pressures, not only becuse of the accumulated Medicaid cuts of the last several years, but because of reductions in payments from private sector payers as well, and our concern is that if you withdraw a couple of billion dollars or more from healthcare, you have a devasting impact on both the quantity and quality of healthcare available."

In its new bill, the Assembly reduced the amount that would be paid by New York State to hospitals by $12.9 million, a fraction of Pataki's proposed $282.6 million reduction, as it turned down plans to limit payments for psychiatric care and emergency room services and freeze inpatient rates.

Nursing homes would see their payments fall by $53.6 million, about a fifth of Pataki's proposed $240.9 million reduction. The home health/and personal care sector would lose $25 million, an area the governor wanted to cut by $136.7 million.

The Assembly refused to go along with his plans to cap how much personal care aides were paid or reduce long-term and home care rates. Changes in benefits and eligibility rules the Asembly wants added up to $4.7 million, roughly one-third of the $14.4 million sum Pataki proposed.

And the Assembly proposed increasing spending in several areas, including healthcare for children, making long-term insurance more accessible, and proposing to spend $40 million on higher capitation rates for Medicaid managed care outfits.
